Photograph: Santiago Saldarriaga/AP View image in fullscreen Residents and rescue workers search the rubble of a collapsed building in Cali, Colombia. Photograph: Santiago Saldarriaga/AP Colombia Scores dead after powerful earthquake strikes western Colombia Quake of 7.4 magnitude collapses and severely damages buildings in several major cities, including Cali and Pereira Colombia earthquake live – latest updates Tom Phillips , and Thomas Graham in Bogotá Mon 10 Aug 2026 14.11 EDT First published on Mon 10 Aug 2026 10.28 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google More than 100 people have died after a powerful earthquake struck western Colombia , collapsing and severely damaging scores of buildings in major cities including Cali and Pereira. The US and Colombian geological surveys reported that a 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck at 7.34am local time (13.34 BST) on Monday, with its epicentre in the western department of Chocó. It was also felt in neighbouring Venezuela, which is still reeling from a deadly double earthquake on 24 June. Colombia’s president, Abelardo de la Espriella ,said 111 people had been killed, 87 injured and 61 buildings collapsed. Western Colombia appears to have suffered the most serious damage, with authorities reporting 27 deaths in the Valle del Cauca department, 40 deaths in Pereira, the capital of Risaralda department, and at least two in Manizales, the capital of Caldas. The mayor of Manizales, Jorge Eduardo Rojas Giraldo, said at least 12 buildings and 20 homes had been partially or completely or destroyed there. Map locating the epicentre of the quake In a social media video, he told citizens to be “completely ready” for aftershocks. “Do not go back into the buildings yet. I know this isn’t easy but stay outside for a little while at least because there could be an aftershock,” he said. Social media videos showed citizens searching for victims in the wreckage of a four-storey hotel in Cali and a woman sprinting from a building as it collapsed in Manizales. One video showed part of San José church in Pereira collapsing as palm trees around it shook. Another video published by the newspaper El Tiempo captured the moment a building gave way in Manizales. View image in fullscreen The cathedral of Manizales was damaged in the quake. Photograph: John Jairo Bonilla/AP The mayor of Cali, Alejandro Eder, said at least 20 buildings had collapsed in his city and that some people were trapped inside. He did not specify how many. “Right now, we are trying to map out what has happened, firstly to protect lives and secondly to be able to push ahead with any kind of rescue that might be necessary,” he said, urging citizens to stay calm. He also told residents to check their buildings for structural damage. “If you do not feel safe, if you see very large cracks, please, leave the building,” he said. The mayor of Pereira, Mauricio Salazar, declared a curfew. In an interview with local radio he said 65 buildings had collapsed, with victims thought to be trapped in at least 15 of them. Five of the city’s hospitals were reportedly inundated with the injured. Buildings damaged after strong earthquake hits Colombia Raúl Andrés Buitrago, the head of customer service at a business in Pereira, described setting off for work when the seismic alert on his watch went off. “There are often little tremors here,” he said. “But I’d never felt an earthquake like this. It started softly, softly, softly, then it felt like it was getting stronger every second.” He spoke of “horrible” scenes as he fled outside onto the street in the city centre, which is home to many old buildings. “The roofs started to fall in. The buildings collapsed in on themselves. The panic was terrible. They were the four longest minutes of my life,” he said. The governor of Chocó, Nubia Carolina Córdoba, said people had been injured and buildings severely damaged in the department’s capital, Quibdó. De la Espriella, who took office on Friday, flew to the capital, Bogotá, where he said he would personally lead the government response. “Colombia has a president whose heart aches for his people and who will do everything in his power to help them in the most difficult moments,” he said in a video posted on his official social networks. His office announced he had ordered an immediate meeting of the national disaster management committee and said the government was “vigilant and in action”. “We will keep Colombians informed,” it said. View image in fullscreen People search the rubble of a collapsed building in Cali. Photograph: Ernesto Guzmán Jr/EPA Aviation authorities said the airports in Pereira, Manizales, Quibdó, Cartago, Armenia and Buenaventura had sustained damage. The earthquake comes weeks after Venezuela was struck by twin earthquakes that devastated the country’s northern coast, killing more than 6,000 people. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said the Trump administration – which has thrown its weight behind Colombia’s new rightwing president – was monitoring the situation closely and stood ready to offer its support. Photograph: US navy/Reuters View image in fullscreen A US sailor directs aircraft on the flight deck of the USS Abraham Lincoln during the ongoing conflict with Iran, on 31 July. Photograph: US navy/Reuters US military US navy veterans and military health experts express concern over USS Abraham Lincoln sailors Prolonged deployment is coupled with reports of water shortages, plumbing issues and attempts to jump overboard Trump downplays concerns about sailors onboard USS Abraham Lincoln Anna Betts Sat 15 Aug 2026 07.00 EDT Last modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 07.25 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google US navy veterans and military health experts are expressing concerns about the strain on sailors aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, which has spent nearly nine months at sea supporting US operations in the Middle East, amid reports of poor living conditions and worsening mental health among its crew. The San Diego-based aircraft carrier left port on 21 November, originally bound for the Pacific, but was redirected to the Middle East as the US-Israel war with Iran began. It has now spent more than 250 consecutive days at sea without a significant port visit, with its deployment repeatedly extended. On Thursday, the Wall Street Journal reported that the US military was preparing to replace the Lincoln with the USS George Washington, as concerns mount over the conditions aboard the Lincoln. Reports by the Navy Times and Stars and Stripes this week described shortages of supplies and water as well as plumbing problems, low morale and deteriorating mental health among the Lincoln’s roughly 5,000 sailors, and further reported that there had been multiple attempts by sailors to jump overboard. The reports prompted several Democratic lawmakers to demand answers from the Pentagon. In response to the reports, a navy official told the Guardian this week that they were aware that “extended deployments place a significant strain on our service members and their families, and we are grateful for the resilience and sacrifices they make” and said that the health and wellbeing of every Lincoln sailor was a priority. “Based on information available to the command, we have not identified an increase in reported suicidal ideation or suicide attempts aboard the ship,” they said, adding that religious, medical and mental health professionals were available as part of a “comprehensive support network” that included “onboard deployment-resilience counselors and chaplains”. The official recognized that the war had disrupted traditional supply hubs, but added that “current reports from the ship confirm continuous access to clean water, functional AC and healthy meal options”. On Thursday, Pete Hegseth claimed that the conditions aboard the Lincoln had been “completely misrepresented”. “We ​make sure that every ship, every crew, every captain has everything we can provide ​them at every single moment,” the US defense secretary told reporters . “Some deployments are longer than others, and ⁠I have more respect and gratitude for those sailors than anybody.” Military experts said on Friday that prolonged deployments, particularly without coming ashore, can place increased strain on both the crew and the ship itself, and noted that extensions can also take a psychological toll by leaving sailors uncertain about when they will return home. Armen Kurdian, a retired US navy captain, who served aboard the Lincoln in 2005, described the carrier as a “giant floating city” with about 5,000 people aboard. “You’re feeding people 15,000 meals per day, you’ve got TV stations, communications,” he said. During his deployment, he said, he took a graduate-level business class remotely, while other sailors found different ways to occupy their downtime. “There’s always something to do,” he said, although he added that life aboard was “certainly high-ops tempo and highly stressful at times”. Sailors live in close quarters, he said, with junior enlisted personnel sleeping in open bay barracks. Kurdian recalled some plumbing problems, including broken toilets, during his deployment, and said that things becoming rusty, dirty or broken can have a “kind of depressing impact on you”. There’s never a time when you’re on the ship and everything’s working perfectly. But, is it happening a lot? “Things break on a ship,” he said. “You’re in the middle of the Gulf, you’re operating, you’ve got aircraft smacking down on decks repeatedly, hundreds of times per day, and that rattles the ship. There’s never a time when you’re on the ship and everything’s going to be working perfectly. But the question is, [is] it happening a lot?” Kurdian said that what surprised him about the Lincoln’s current deployment was not its length, but the amount of time the crew had gone without a significant port visit. “That will take a toll on people when you don’t get to stand on dry land for a while,” he said. Robert Murrett, a retired US navy vice-admiral, said that a typical aircraft-carrier deployment is closer to six months and normally includes port visits that allow sailors to rest and spend some time away from the ship. The Lincoln, Murrett said, “has had none of that since they left San Diego last November”. “They’ve been under way for that very, very long period of time, approaching nine months, and they’ve also been under combat conditions for much [of it] because of their time in the Middle East,” he said. “That’s very, very tough on a crew.” Murrett described life aboard an aircraft carrier as “tough”, calling it a “huge, compressed environment”, where there is “a lot of stress” and it can be a “very dangerous environment”. Earlier this year, the USS Gerald R Ford aircraft carrier returned home after a 326-day deployment, marking the longest US carrier deployment since the Vietnam war . That deployment had reports of a fire and complaints about food shortages. Nancy Lacore, a three-star navy rear admiral who served in the navy for 35 years, said in a statement that during her first deployment, she was “operating in that same region as the USS Abraham Lincoln”. “Just like those sailors, when we left our home port on deployment, we knew when we were supposed to come home,” said Lacore, who was ousted by Hegseth in August during his purge of senior US military officials and who is now running for Congress in South Carolina. “We had an end date, and we were counting down to it.” “Then something changed in the region and just as we thought we were heading home, our ship turned around and went back to the Gulf,” she said. “I still remember how mentally crushing it was to realize the date you’ve been holding onto is gone.” People aboard the Lincoln, she said, have “experienced that uncertainty repeatedly”. “Our Sailors are tough and resilient,” she added. “But their resilience shouldn’t be taken for granted or used as an excuse to keep asking more of them without a clear end in sight.” Our sailors are tough and resilient. But that shouldn’t be used as an excuse to ask for more without a clear end in sight Terri Tanielian, a senior behavioral scientist who has studied deployments and their impact on troops and families, said that prolonged separations are difficult, but that uncertainty over when a deployment will end can make the strain worse. “When families know what they’re planning for, or when an individual knows what they’re planning for … then that is an expectation that they can set themselves up to manage,” she said. But when those expectations change unexpectedly, she said, “like we saw, for example, in 2008, 2009 and 2010 timeframes, and with the deployments there, where we had to keep people for longer, we also saw some increases in the mental strain that the units were facing”, referring to both troops and their families. Responding to the reports about the conditions aboard the Lincoln, Tanielian said it was “heartbreaking to think about the struggles that folks are facing and to feel that they’re kind of feeling that desperate and isolated and perhaps not supported”. Support, she said, needs to extend beyond just ensuring access to psychological support: “It’s also about, are they getting enough sleep? Are they getting reset opportunities? Are they getting the opportunity to exercise? How are we helping them maintain their overall wellbeing?” Explore more on these topics US military US-Israel war on Iran Trump administration US politics US foreign policy news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

https://telex.hu/karakter/kultura/2026/0.text: Menü Kereső Reisz Gábor legújabb filmjét vetítjük premier előtt a Telex Filmklubon Kultúra Klág Dávid Reisz Gábort már valószínűleg nem kell bemutatni a magyar mozinézőknek, a Van valami furcsa és megmagyarázhatatlan milleniál közérzeti filmjétől kezdve a Magyarázat mindenre politikai tipródásáig bezárólag ő volt az a rendező, aki nemcsak egy szűk réteg, hanem konkrétan százezrek számára készített filmeket – egy kivétel nélkül komolyabb állami támogatás nélkül . A Magyarázat mindenre a velencei filmfesztivál Orizzonti-szekciójában elnyerte a fődíjat a premierjén , a legújabb, Földszint című filmje pedig szintén az olasz fesztiválon mutatkozik be idén. És nem sokkal az olasz premier után, de még bőven a magyar premier előtt egy Telex Filmklub keretében mi is meg tudjuk majd mutatni a filmet, ráadásul utána a rendező, Reisz Gábor is ott lesz velünk. A Földszint a hivatalos leírása a következő: A tragikomédia főszereplője Méhn Kristóf, a festőművészből lett banki archiváló, aki feleségével, Verával egy társasházi földszinti lakásban lakik. A történet azon a napon játszódik, amikor Kristóf véletlenül penészfoltot fedez fel lakásuk falán, és nem sokkal később megtudja Verától, hogy gyerekük lesz. Elhatározza, hogy felderíti a penész eredetét. A korábban számára ismeretlen lakótársak faggatása közben egyre élesebbé válik a konfliktusa a nyájaskodó közös képviselővel, aki épp egy nagy liftbeszerelési projektet akar keresztülvinni a késő délutáni lakógyűlésen. Ahogy Kristóf kezd belegabalyodni a ház ügyeibe, gyanúja egyre erősebb: a ház beteg. A filmet szeptember 20-án 20:30-kor vetítjük a budapesti Puskin moziban. A film 107 perces, utána Reisz Gáborral lesz egy beszélgetés. Jegyet itt lehet rá venni. A Földszint október 1-jén kerül forgalmazásba a magyar mozikban a Cirko jóvoltából. https://euobserver.com/242944/train-cont.text: The series continues as we report on developments following April’s historic election and on the steps taken since then by the Tisza government. This week, we cover the following topics: Another blow for Hungary’s richest man; New chief prosecutor nominee, plus a former chief prosecutor ready to testify on political pressure; Parliament has adopted the new child-protection law; A state secretary has unexpectedly left the government; Orbán to keep quiet on one of Hungary’s most important national holidays; Ukraine adopts the minority education law; More EU funds and money from the Norway Grants have become available. Another blow for Lőrinc Mészáros Last Friday (9 October), prime minister Péter Magyar and Dávid Vitézy, minister for transport and investments, announced that the state was suspending implementation of one of Hungary’s largest rail projects – the Budapest southern circular railway, and will launch a new public procurement procedure. The works had been carried out by V-Híd, the most profitable company of Lőrinc Mészáros, who became Hungary’s richest man during Viktor Orbán’s premiership. However, the European Court of Auditors uncovered serious public-procurement irregularities: V-Híd may have colluded with the company that drafted the project plans and thus already possessed information at the time of the tender that its competitors did not have. Because of this, the European Court of Auditors would withdraw EU funding from the project. The Hungarian government does not want to forfeit the EU money and make Hungarian taxpayers foot the bill for the costs of the project, which is why it is terminating the contract with Mészáros’s company and launching a new tender. The Hungarian state had already taken away from Mészáros the right to operate a motorway section, and later also terminated the 35-year motorway concession. Previously, one of his food-industry companies had EU funding already granted to it withdrawn, while his energy company was excluded from a call for proposals financed from the repatriated RRF funds. New chief prosecutor nominee, plus former chief prosecutor ready to testify On Monday (12 October), president András Baka nominated a former chief prosecutor, Péter Fejes, for the post of chief prosecutor. His first nominee, Zoltán Szathmáry, was not voted through by the Tisza group in parliament after it emerged that his brother was implicated in the so-called gold convoy case, in which a Ukrainian cash shipment was stopped and confiscated by the Hungarian authorities. Fejes was dismissed in 2012 from his position as chief prosecutor of Vas county by Péter Polt, the chief prosecutor serving the Orbán system, citing loss of confidence. Since then he has continued to work within the prosecution service and as a university lecturer, and he has no party affiliation. For the time being neither prime minister Magyar nor the Tisza group has stated whether they support Fejes’s nomination. Since the change of government, another former chief prosecutor, Pál Fürcht, has frequently spoken to the media. Among other things, he has claimed that the gold convoy case was created for political purposes, and that the authorities raided the Ukrainian cash couriers on Orbán ’s orders. On Sunday (11 October), Magyar sharply criticised Fürcht in a Facebook post, reproaching him for having been a servant of the system himself. According to Magyar, Fürcht constructed a criminal case, on political orders, out of the notorious nightclub altercation for which the prime minister is currently under investigation on charges of theft. Read more Magyar waives his own immunity, as Hungary targets billions in alleged fraud and two former Orbán ministers in custody (Day 143 of the Tisza government) It was likewise Fürcht who left former propaganda minister Antal Rogán out of the corruption case known as the Völner–Schadl affair. In response to Magyar’s criticism, Fürcht said he was ready to make an official statement before any authority. In parliament on Monday, the prime minister was already referring to the former chief prosecutor as a future witness. Parliament has adopted the new child-protection law Child protection was one of the most important topics of the campaign and played a major role in Orbán’s downfall. Magyar kept the issue on the agenda even after his government took office; most recently, last Thursday, the prime minister and the state secretary responsible for the field, Szilvia Gyurkó, presented the report on the children’s home in Bicske. This home had been run by a director who was decorated by Orbán and later convicted of paedophile crimes, together with his deputy, who helped cover up the abuses. The presidential pardon granted to the deputy shook the Orbán government and helped lead to its collapse. On Tuesday (13 October), parliament adopted an amendment to the child-protection law, which takes a tougher stance against media content accessible to minors that propagates sexual violence, manipulation and exploitation, and would speed up the placement of babies abandoned in hospital. The amendment removed those homophobic passages that the Orbán government forced into law in 2021, and which the Court of Justice of the European Union also ruled to be contrary to EU law. Fidesz, the Christian Democratic People’s Party (KDNP) and the far-right Mi Hazánk did not vote for the amendment; Magyar called this a disgrace. A state secretary unexpectedly leaves the government On Tuesday, András Tótth, state secretary for energy at the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Energy and minister István Kapitány’s most important aide, unexpectedly resigned.
